items.title: The earliest Christians thought Jesus would return within their lifetime
items.claim: Paul's letters (50s CE) are the oldest Christian texts. What does he tell his churches about the timing of Christ's return?

options.text: He explicitly warns that it will be many centuries away
He tells believers — in 1 Thessalonians 4 and 1 Corinthians 15 — that 'we who are alive, who are left' will be caught up to meet the Lord
He refuses to discuss the timing at all
He places the return precisely at AD 70, the destruction of the Temple

items.reveal:
1 Thessalonians 4:15-17, written around 50-51 CE, includes Paul among those still alive at the Parousia. 1 Corinthians 7:29 says 'the appointed time has grown short.' Mark 9:1 has Jesus saying 'some standing here will not taste death' before seeing the Kingdom.

When Christ did not return, later texts (e.g. 2 Peter 3:8 — 'one day is with the Lord as a thousand years') reinterpret the delay. This shift is one of the central transformations of early Christian theology.
items.why: Treating the New Testament as a unified, settled doctrine misses that it documents a community reinterpreting itself in real time. The 'delay of the Parousia' is one of the formative pressures on Christian thought.

items.title: Theravada and Mahayana are two major Buddhist traditions
items.claim: What distinguishes the major Buddhist schools?

options.text: There are no real differences between Buddhist schools

Theravada ('teaching of the elders', dominant in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia, Laos) emphasises individual liberation through the Pali Canon; Mahayana (East Asia, Vietnam) emphasises the bodhisattva path and includes Pure Land, Zen and Tibetan (Vajrayana) traditions
Theravada is Buddhist; Mahayana is a separate religion

items.reveal:
The split developed in the centuries after the Buddha's death, with the Second Council (around 100 years after his parinirvana) marking early disagreements. Mahayana texts (Prajnaparamita Sutras, Lotus Sutra) emerged from around the 1st century BCE.

The bodhisattva ideal — postponing one's own final liberation to help all beings — is central to Mahayana. Theravada acknowledges bodhisattvas (including the historical Buddha before his enlightenment) but emphasises the arhat ideal (the awakened practitioner).

Tibetan Buddhism is sometimes treated as a separate Vajrayana branch. Zen and Pure Land are East Asian Mahayana developments.
items.why: Calling Buddhism 'one religion' obscures real diversity. Theravada and Mahayana share core teachings but differ on the path, the goal, the texts treated as authoritative, and the role of devotion.
